summary.text: Encode the configuration by tail masses \(F(n,t,i)\); mass conservation and positivity show that stabilization is equivalent to \(F(n,t,n-1)>0\), and the averaging recurrence also gives eventual positivity. Inductive shift estimates for that recurrence show \(F(n+1,t+1,i+1)\le F(n,t,i)\) and that \(F(n,t,i)>0\) implies \(F(n+1,t+2,i+1)>0\), so the two minimal stabilization times are separated by at least one and at most two steps.

full_proof.text:
Let a configuration be a finite list of nonnegative integers. In one step, a cell of mass \(m\) keeps
\[
\left\lceil \frac m2\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor
\]
and sends \(\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) to the cell immediately to its right. Thus, if the current configuration is \((c_0,\ldots,c_{r-1})\), the untrimmed next configuration is
\[
\left(
\left\lceil\frac{c_0}{2}\right\rceil,
\left\lceil\frac{c_1}{2}\right\rceil+\left\lfloor\frac{c_0}{2}\right\rfloor,
\ldots,
\left\lceil\frac{c_{r-1}}2\right\rceil+\left\lfloor\frac{c_{r-2}}2\right\rfloor,
\left\lfloor\frac{c_{r-1}}2\right\rfloor
\right),
\]
after which trailing zeroes are deleted. Denote by \(S(n,t)\) the configuration obtained after \(t\) steps from the one-cell configuration \((n)\).

We will encode a configuration by its tail masses. For a finite list \(C=(c_0,c_1,\ldots)\), put
\[
T_C(i)=\sum_{j\ge i}c_j,
\]
where the sum is zero once \(i\) is beyond the end of the list. Define integers \(F(n,t,i)\) recursively by
\[
F(n,0,0)=n,\qquad F(n,0,i)=0\quad(i>0),
\]
\[
F(n,t,0)=n\quad(t\ge 0),
\]
and
\[
F(n,t+1,i+1)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{F(n,t,i)+F(n,t,i+1)}2\right\rfloor.
\tag{1}
\]
We first establish that these are precisely the tail masses of the automaton:
\[
T_{S(n,t)}(i)=F(n,t,i).
\tag{2}
\]

To see this, first note that a step preserves total mass, because
\[
\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil+\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor=m
\]
for every integer \(m\), and deleting trailing zeroes does not affect any tail sum. Now consider the tail beginning at position \(i+1\) after one step. It consists of the mass sent rightward from positions \(i,i+1,\ldots\), together with the mass retained at positions \(i+1,i+2,\ldots\). Hence, writing \(C\) for the old configuration,
\[
T_{\operatorname{step}(C)}(i+1)
 =\sum_{j\ge i}\left\lfloor\frac{c_j}{2}\right\rfloor
  +\sum_{j\ge i+1}\left\lceil\frac{c_j}{2}\right\rceil.
\]
For every \(j\ge i+1\), the two contributions belonging to \(c_j\) add to \(c_j\). Therefore this is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{c_i}{2}\right\rfloor+T_C(i+1).
\]
Since \(T_C(i)=c_i+T_C(i+1)\), this equals
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{T_C(i)+T_C(i+1)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
Indeed, the numerator is \(c_i+2T_C(i+1)\). Together with conservation of total mass, this proves (2) by induction on \(t\), using (1). In particular,
\[
\sum S(n,t)=F(n,t,0)=n.
\tag{3}
\]

For \(n>0\), every entry of every configuration \(S(n,t)\) is positive. This is true initially. If all old entries are positive, then the first new entry, \(\lceil c_0/2\rceil\), is positive, as is every subsequent entry that receives the positive retained part \(\lceil c_j/2\rceil\). The possible final entry \(\lfloor c_{r-1}/2\rfloor\) is either positive or is a trailing zero and is deleted. Thus positivity is preserved.

This gives a useful exact criterion for stability. For \(n>0\),
\[
S(n,t)=(1,1,\ldots,1)\text{ (with \(n\) entries)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F(n,t,n-1)>0.
\tag{4}
\]
For the forward implication, the tail starting at index \(n-1\) of the all-ones list is \(1\), so (2) gives the desired positivity. Conversely, suppose \(F(n,t,n-1)>0\). By (2), the tail of \(S(n,t)\) beginning at position \(n-1\) is positive, so the list has length at least \(n\). On the other hand, all its entries are positive integers and its sum is \(n\) by (3), so its length is at most \(n\). Its length is therefore exactly \(n\), and \(n\) positive integers with sum \(n\) must all equal \(1\). This proves (4).

We next prove the comparison properties of \(F\) that drive the argument. All divisions below are integer divisions, i.e. floors.

First, \(F\) is nonincreasing in its last index:
\[
F(n,t,i+1)\le F(n,t,i).
\tag{5}
\]
This follows by induction on \(t\). At time zero it is immediate. At a later time and away from index zero, both sides are obtained from adjacent sums in (1), and the induction hypothesis says each term in the sum for the left side is at most the corresponding term in the sum for the right side. At the boundary, (1) gives
\[
F(n,t+1,1)=\left\lfloor\frac{n+F(n,t,1)}2\right\rfloor\le n=F(n,t+1,0),
\]
because the induction hypothesis gives \(F(n,t,1)\le F(n,t,0)=n\).

Second, increasing the initial mass cannot decrease a tail:
\[
F(n,t,i)\le F(n+1,t,i).
\tag{6}
\]
Again this is an immediate induction on \(t\): it is clear initially and at index zero, and (1) preserves inequalities because addition and integer division by two are monotone.

From (1) and (6) we obtain the half-shift lower estimate
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{F(n,t,i)}2\right\rfloor
 \le F(n+1,t+1,i+1).
\tag{7}
\]
Indeed, the right side is
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{F(n+1,t,i)+F(n+1,t,i+1)}2
\right\rfloor,
\]
whose numerator is at least \(F(n,t,i)\).

We also need the opposite, unhalved shifted estimate
\[
F(n+1,t+1,i+1)\le F(n,t,i).
\tag{8}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At \(t=0\), if \(i=0\), the assertion is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n+1}{2}\right\rfloor\le n,
\]
which holds for the positive values of \(n\) used below (and also in the only exceptional zero case after direct inspection); for \(i>0\), both relevant tails on the right are zero and the assertion is immediate. For the induction step, first consider \(i=0\). By the induction hypothesis,
\[
F(n+1,t+1,1)\le F(n,t,0)=n,
\]
and hence
\[
F(n+1,t+2,1)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n+1+F(n+1,t+1,1)}2\right\rfloor
 \le n=F(n,t+1,0).
\]
For \(i>0\), apply (1) to both sides. The two terms in the numerator on the left are bounded by the two corresponding terms on the right by the induction hypothesis, proving (8).

The crucial strict comparison is
\[
F(n,t,i)=0
\quad\text{or}\quad
F(n,t,i)<F(n+1,t+1,i).
\tag{9}
\]
We prove it by induction on \(t\). At time zero, it is clear: at index zero it says \(n<n+1\), while at every positive index the first alternative holds. The index-zero case at any later time is again \(n<n+1\).

It remains to perform the induction step at a positive index. Set
\[
X=F(n,t,i),\qquad Z=F(n,t,i+1),
\]
\[
Y=F(n+1,t+1,i),\qquad W=F(n+1,t+1,i+1).
\]
We must compare
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{X+Z}{2}\right\rfloor
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{Y+W}{2}\right\rfloor.
\tag{10}
\]
If \(Z>0\), then (9) at indices \(i\) and \(i+1\), together with (5) if needed to exclude \(X=0\), gives
\[
X<Y,\qquad Z<W.
\]
Thus \(X+Z+2\le Y+W\), and consequently
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{X+Z}{2}\right\rfloor
 <\left\lfloor\frac{Y+W}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]

Suppose instead that \(Z=0\). If also \(X=0\), the left side of (10) is zero, giving the first alternative in (9). If \(X>0\), the induction hypothesis gives \(X<Y\), hence \(X+1\le Y\), while (7) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac X2\right\rfloor\le W.
\]
Therefore
\[
X+1+\left\lfloor\frac X2\right\rfloor\le Y+W.
\tag{11}
\]
For a positive integer \(X\), (11) implies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac X2\right\rfloor
 <\left\lfloor\frac{Y+W}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
This is elementary: if \(q=\lfloor X/2\rfloor\), then \(X\ge q+1\), so the right side of (11) is at least \(2q+2\), and its half-floor is at least \(q+1\). Since \(Z=0\), the left side of (10) is \(q\). This completes the proof of (9).

An immediate consequence of (9) is the following two-step propagation of positivity:
\[
F(n,t,i)>0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
F(n+1,t+2,i+1)>0.
\tag{12}
\]
Indeed, (9) gives
\[
F(n+1,t+1,i)>F(n,t,i)>0,
\]
so in fact \(F(n+1,t+1,i)\ge2\). Applying (1),
\[
F(n+1,t+2,i+1)
 =\left\lfloor
 \frac{F(n+1,t+1,i)+F(n+1,t+1,i+1)}2
 \right\rfloor\ge1.
\]

Before taking a least stabilization time, we verify that stabilization does occur. We claim that for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
F(n,2(n-1),n-1)>0.
\tag{13}
\]
This is an induction on \(n\). For \(n=1\), it is \(F(1,0,0)=1\). If it holds for \(n\), apply (12) with \(t=2(n-1)\) and \(i=n-1\). We get
\[
F(n+1,2(n-1)+2,n)>0,
\]
which is exactly (13) for \(n+1\), since \(2(n-1)+2=2n\). By (4), mass \(n\) is therefore stable by time \(2(n-1)\).

Let \(A(n)\) be the least time at which the mass-\(n\) automaton is the stable list of \(n\) ones (and put \(A(0)=0\)). The existence just proved shows that this least time is well-defined for every positive \(n\). By definition,
\[
S(n,A(n))=(1,\ldots,1),
\tag{14}
\]
and whenever \(S(n,t)=(1,\ldots,1)\), we have
\[
A(n)\le t.
\tag{15}
\]
By (4), (14) is equivalent to
\[
F(n,A(n),n-1)>0.
\tag{16}
\]

We can now bound \(A(n+1)\) in terms of \(A(n)\). Fix \(n\ge1\). Apply (12) to (16), with \(t=A(n)\) and \(i=n-1\). This gives
\[
F(n+1,A(n)+2,n)>0.
\]
By the stability criterion (4), the mass-\(n+1\) automaton is stable at time \(A(n)+2\). Therefore, by minimality,
\[
A(n+1)\le A(n)+2.
\tag{17}
\]

For the lower bound, write \(A(n+1)=t+1\). This representation is legitimate because \(A(n+1)\ne0\): at time zero the mass-\(n+1\) configuration has only one cell, while \(n+1\ge2\); equivalently, its tail at index \(n\) is zero, contradicting the positive-tail criterion for stability.

Since mass \(n+1\) is stable at time \(t+1\), (4) gives
\[
F(n+1,t+1,n)>0.
\]
Apply the shifted upper estimate (8) with index \(n-1\):
\[
F(n+1,t+1,n)\le F(n,t,n-1).
\]
Thus \(F(n,t,n-1)>0\), so (4) says that the mass-\(n\) automaton is already stable at time \(t\). By minimality,
\[
A(n)\le t,
\]
and hence
\[
A(n)+1\le t+1=A(n+1).
\tag{18}
\]

Combining (17) and (18),
\[
A(n)+1\le A(n+1)\le A(n)+2.
\]
All quantities are integers, so necessarily
\[
A(n+1)=A(n)+1
\quad\text{or}\quad
A(n+1)=A(n)+2.
\]
The function \(A(n)\) is exactly the sequence \(a(n)\) from the statement, since both are defined as the least number of applications of the stated halving-and-transfer rule required to reach the list of \(n\) unit cells. Therefore, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
as claimed.
